title: Araneofauna (Arachnida: Araneae) da trilha ecológica do Centro de Estudos Costeiros Limnológicos e Marinhos (CECLIMAR), Rio Grande do Sul, Brasil
venue: Lume (Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul)
abstract: As aranhas atuam no controle biológico e incluem espécies de importância médica. O Litoral Norte do Rio Grande do Sul permanece pouco amostrado quanto à sua araneofauna, o que demanda inventários padronizados. Este trabalho realizou um levantamento na Trilha Ecológica do CECLIMAR, em Imbé-RS, para identificar as espécies presentes e caracterizar a diversidade em cinco pontos de mata aberta e fechada e em seus microambientes. Por se tratar de uma pesquisa do tipo exploratória, não é baseada em hipótese. As coletas ocorreram mensalmente entre fevereiro de 2023 e janeiro de 2024, com exceção de junho, agosto e novembro, quando as condições meteorológicas impediram a amostragem. Utilizaram-se guarda-chuva entomológico e busca ativa (análise livre visual e análise em ambientes especiais). O material foi triado sob estereomicroscópio, conservado em álcool 70% e posteriormente, identificados em nível de família com uso de chave dicotômica e separados em “morfoespécies”. Foram elaboradas curvas de rarefação para avaliar a suficiência amostral e diagramas de Venn para comparar as famílias de aranhas entre os pontos amostrados e identificar possíveis exclusividades por local ou método de coleta. Nas nove coletas foram obtidos 365 indivíduos e 20 famílias foram identificadas, sendo cerca de 26% do total (95) aranhas adultas, pertencentes a 15 famílias. As famílias mais abundantes (incluindo jovens) foram: Theridiidae (17,81%), Salticidae (14,52%), Thomisidae (13,97%), Araneidae (11,78%) e Anyphaenidae (11,78%). Por meio do uso do guarda-chuva entomológico foram coletados 69,6% dos indivíduos, enquanto a coleta ativa foi responsável por 30,4% das coletas. Ambas as metodologias registraram nove famílias em comum, enquanto dez famílias foram exclusivas da coleta ativa e uma foi registrada apenas pelo guarda-chuva entomológico. Todos os pontos amostrados apresentaram ao menos uma família exclusiva, com exceção do ponto quatro. O verão foi a estação que apresentou a maior abundância de indivíduos adultos (30) além do maior número total de indivíduos (126), seguido pelo outono (122) e primavera (61), enquanto o inverno (56) foi a estação menos representativa. A riqueza de famílias foi mais elevada na primavera (17). A curva de rarefação demonstra que o esforço amostral empregado foi adequado para estimar a riqueza da comunidade, uma vez que a curva tende à estabilização. Isso sugere que a maioria das famílias presentes foi registrada e que novas coletas tenderiam a adicionar poucas famílias novas à lista. A trilha ecológica do CECLIMAR apresentou araneofauna diversificada nos diferentes biótopos amostrados. A metodologia de coleta empregada se mostrou eficiente para a investigação dessa diversidade, permitindo obtenção rápida de espécimes para o levantamento faunístico. Na continuação deste trabalho os espécimes serão determinados a nível de gênero, considerando a ocorrência desses táxons no estado do RS com base na literatura científica pertinente.

title: Arthropod Daily Visits to Zinnia elegans and Ruellia tuberosa in Megaluh District
abstract: Arthropod daily visits were seen from how often the Arthropod family visited the refugia plants of Zinnia elegans and Ruellia tuberosa species which were determined based on the Arthropod average per hour observed. This study aims to (1) find out what arthropods are found in Zinnia elegans and Ruellia tuberosa in Megaluh District, (2) find out the frequency of daily visits of arthropods to Zinnia elegans and Ruellia tuberosa plants in Megaluh District. This research is an exploratory descriptive study with a quantitative approach. This research was conducted in February 2021. Determination of the sampling point (sampling) was determined using the purposive sampling technique. The technique of collecting data is by collecting data using the visual control method at a distance of 2 meters at 06.00-07-00, 11.00-12.00, and 16.00-17.00. The data analysis technique was using SPSS paired t-test (pair-sample t-test). The results showed 22 families were found consisting of Paradoxosomatidae, Calliphoridae, Formicidae, Salticidae, Muscidae, Pentatomidae, Apidae, Vespidae, Flatidae, Gryllidae, Chrysomelidae, Crambidae, Hesperiidae, Stratiomyidae, Oxypidae, Coenagrionidae, Mantidae, Alyphecidae, Coccinellidae, Coccinellidae. , Pieridae. The highest average daily visitation frequency for Zinnia elegans was the Formicidae family with an average daily visit frequency of 8.5556 individuals/hour, while the highest family Ruellia tuberosa was also the Formicidae family with an average of 14.3333 individuals/hour. In Zinnia elegans and Ruellia tuberosa based on t-test, the significance level (2-tailed) was significant in the Pentatomidae family with a significance value of 0.003.

title: Exploring the diversity and species richness of the arachnid community in rice agroecosystems with differing management practices in Central Kerala, South India
abstract: The Kuttanad region of Kerala, a below-sea-level rice agroecosystem within the Vembanad-Kol Wetland (a Ramsar site), represents a unique but fragile habitat with high ecological value. This study involved the collection of 130 spiders over 3 years using sweeping nets, visual collection, and pitfall traps. Spider diversity was assessed across four sample sites, two organic farms and two pesticide-using farms. Species from 86 genera and 22 families were recorded, with Salticidae, Araneidae, and Tetragnathidae being the most species-rich families. Guild analysis revealed seven functional groups, with stalkers and orb-weavers predominating. Diversity indices (Shannon H: 4.178 and 4.092 in organic farms vs. 3.602 and 3.254 in pesticide-using farms) and richness estimators (Chao1: 132–140 vs. 84–91 species) indicated significantly higher diversity in organic systems. Bray-Curtis similarity and dendrogram analyses showed distinct species assemblages in organic vs. conventional farms, reflecting the influence of agricultural practices. Seasonal analyses demonstrated that several families persisted year-round, recolonizing fields during non-cultivation periods. The high species richness, functional diversity, and resilience of spider communities underscore their importance as natural pest regulators in rice ecosystems. The findings highlight that organic farming practices enhance biodiversity conservation, making them a crucial strategy for maintaining ecological balance in wetland agroecosystems.

title: APLIKASI BIOINSEKTISIDA CAIR BERBAHAN AKTIF Metarhizium anisopliae PADA TANAMAN PADI DAN PENGARUHNYA TERHADAP SERANGGA HAMA DAN ARTHROPODA PREDATOR DI LAHAN PADI RAWA LEBAK
abstract: Pest control by the use of synthetic insecticides being excessive and not according to forego agriculture department can be harmful for the environment, this could lead to a negative impact as pest resistance target and the occurrence of resurgensi inflict pests . This research aims to understand population insect pests and arthropods having at predatory give treatment made bioinsecticide M. anisopliae on the rice plant. The research was conducted in rice field land lebak at Pelabuhan Dalam village, Kecamatan Pemulutan, ogan ilir district, province of south sumatra. Making of bioinsectixide did at laboratory entomology of pest and a disease of the faculty agricultural of sriwijaya university, indralaya. This research start from on july 2015 to november 2015. Methods used to this research is the method random design group, which consisted of 6 treatment and 5 repeating. Those who used consist of 100 mL M. anisopliae + 600 mL EKKU sterile, 100 mL Pelet M. anisopliae + 600 mL EKKU sterile, 100 mL M. anisopliae + 600 mL EKKU non sterile, 100 mL GYB M. anisopliae, Extract Compost the Skin Shrimp ( EKKU ), Water (Control), in this research insects pests are found dominant in the rice field area at Pelabuhan Dalam village is Nephotettix virescens (Leafhoppers Green), Cofana spectra (Leafhoppers White), Leptocorisa acuta ( Leafhoppers an order of insects), Nezara viridula (Ladybugs Green), Scirporphaga incertulas (Stalk Borer Rice Yellow), Oxya cinendis (Locusts Paddy), Acrida turiita (Locusts Pocong). The arthropods predators most common to find in land of rice at Pelabuhan Dalam village either through the observation a net or the visual observation is the family from Tetragnathidae, Oxyopidae, Coccinelidae and Staphylinidae. The Conclusions from this research show that a paddy plant applied bioinsectixide active made Metarhizium anisopliae not had have real impact in reducing population of insect pests to reduce damage of paddy plants, the application were not a bad impact for abundance and diversity of arthropods predators, paddy plants applied by bioinsectixide active made Metarhizium anisopliae have no real impact on increased produce of paddy.

title: Habrocestoides shuqiangi Wang & Mi 2025, sp. nov.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Habrocestoides shuqiangi Wang & Mi, sp. nov. Figures 1A–C, 2A–G Type material. Holotype: ♂ (TRU-JS 0853), CHINA: Xizang Autonomous Region: Dinggye County, Chentang Township, Natang Village (27°52.43'N, 87°24.87'E, 2390 m a.s.l.), 27.V.2025, leg. C. Wang et al. Paratype: 1♀ (TRU-JS 0854), same data as for holotype. Etymology. The specific name is a patronym in honour of Dr Shuqiang Li, one of the leading spider taxonomists worldwide; noun (name) in genitive case. Diagnosis. The male of the new species resembles that of H. indicus Prószyński, 1992 in having a similar palpal structure, but can be easily distinguished by the following aspects: (1) the compound terminal apophysis is retrolateral to the embolus and the tip extends beyond the embolic tip (Fig. 1B) vs mostly overlapping with the embolus and the tip not extending beyond the embolic tip in H. indicus (Prószyński 1992: fig. 45); and (2) the tegular cleft is transverse (Fig. 1B) vs oblique in H. indicus (Prószyński 1992: fig. 45). The female of this new species can be easily distinguished from other congeners by the location of the spermathecae, which are posterior to the origins of the copulatory ducts (Fig. 2B) vs anterior to the origins of the copulatory ducts in other congeners (Logunov 1999: figs 18, 20, 23). Description. Male (Holotype, Figs 1A–C, 2C, E–G). Total length 3.91. Carapace 2.02 long, 1.47 wide.Abdomen 1.79 long, 1.28 wide. Eye sizes and interdistances: AME 0.45, ALE 0.29, PLE 0.26, AERW 1.40, PERW 1.26, EFL 0.91. Legs: I 6.16 (1.83, 1.03, 1.55, 1.10, 0.65), II 4.08 (1.25, 0.73, 0.90, 0.75, 0.45), III 4.11 (1.25, 0.63, 0.90, 0.88, 0.45), IV 5.42 (1.48, 0.93, 1.18, 1.25, 0.58). Carapace dark brown to dark, covered with dense golden and dark setae on cephalon, with central, dark yellow stripe occupying anterior half of thorax; fovea dark red, linear. Chelicerae with typical dentition for most of salticids, two promarginal teeth and one retromarginal tooth. Endites dark yellow, widened distally, with pale disto-inner areas clothed with dense dark setae. Labium darker than endites. Sternum almost oval, about as long as wide, with straight anterior edge. Legs slender, pale yellow to dark, with three and two pairs of ventral spines on tibiae and metatarsi I, respectively. Dorsum of abdomen spotted, brown mingled with irregular dark patches, with anteromedian scutum, and two pairs of anteromedian muscle depressions; venter mainly dark, with irregular pale grey patches and small dots. Palp (Fig. 1A–C): tibia slightly longer than wide, with almost oval distoprolateral concave; retrolateral tibial apophysis widened at base, then acutely narrowed into strongly sclerotized, subtriangular portion with blunt end; cymbium about 1.9 times longer than wide; tegulum slightly swollen, with posterior lobe extending downward; embolus strongly sclerotized, almost bar-shaped; compound terminal apophysis retrolateral to embolus, somewhat longer than embolus, with prolateral membranous portion, and blunt tip. Female (TRU-JS 0854, Fig. 2A, B, D). Total length 3.26. Carapace 1.62 long, 1.26 wide. Abdomen 1.74 long, 1.10 wide. Eye sizes and interdistances: AME 0.38, ALE 0.24, PLE 0.21, AERW 1.15, PERW 1.12, EFL 0.79. Legs: I 3.39 (1.03, 0.63, 0.78, 0.55, 0.40), II 3.03 (0.95, 0.55, 0.65, 0.50, 0.38), III 3.37 (0.98, 0.50, 0.73, 0.73, 0.43), IV 4.22 (1.25, 0.53, 0.98, 0.98, 0.48). Habitus (Fig. 2D) similar to that of male, except paler in color and without dorsal abdominal scutum. Epigyne (Fig. 2A, B): more than 1.5 times wider than long, with subtriangular basal plate possessing posterior, oval structure; atrium almost 1.8 times wider than long, with pair of anterior, arc-shaped ridges; copulatory openings beneath lateral portions of atrial ridges; copulatory ducts flat, curved to C-shapes at origin, then strongly curved and followed by more sclerotized portions connected to median inner margins of spermathecae; spermathecae oblique bar-shaped, ca 2.8 times longer than wide, almost touching each other; fertilization ducts originate from anterior portions of spermathecae. Distribution. Known only from the type locality in Xizang, China (Fig. 9).

title: Revendo o problema da detecção de retas através dos olhos da aranha.
abstract: Visão é um processo que envolve uma grande quantidade de informações, as quais precisam ser otimizadas de alguma forma para propiciar um processamento eficiente. Grande parte das informações visuais estão contidas nos contornos de uma imagem e uma grande redução no volume dos dados pode ser conseguida com a análise dos contornos. Além dos contornos, a detecção de segmentos de reta é o próximo passo na compressão das informações visuais. A detecção de retas ocorre no sistema visual humano, e também no de outros seres vivos. Entre os invertebrados terrestres, o melhor sistema de visão é o das aranhas da família Salticidae e este apresenta características que facilitam a detecção de retas. Este trabalho propõe um novo método de detecção de retas, baseado no sistema visual das aranhas saltadoras, que aborda este problema através de um enfoque inédito, por otimização. O método realiza a busca por retas através de janelas lineares. Para isso, a detecção de retas será feita em um espaço de parâmetros, com a utilização do algoritmo de maximização de funções \\"Downhill Simplex\\". O método desenvolvido leva em consideração a natureza discreta da imagem e do espaço de parâmetros utilizado, e este trabalho inclui um estudo detalhado destes espaços discretos. O método incorpora, para lidar adequadamente com as peculiaridades do problema, características como \\"Simulated Annealing\\" e largura adaptativa. O desempenho do método depende de um conjunto de parâmetros cujo comportamento é de difícil previsão, e a escolha de um conjunto foi realizada através de um algoritmo genético. O trabalho envolve também a construção de um protótipo para a realização de testes utilizando o método desenvolvido. Os resultados foram analisados quanto a precisão na detecção de retas, ao tempo de processamento e a movimentação das janelas lineares, relacionada aos esforços na busca por retas.

title: The Bugs of America 1826–1838
abstract: The first time I saw the original print of John James Audubon’s portrait of the yellow-billed cuckoo from his The Birds of America series (Fig. 1), I was startled by its size. The print is on a sheet of paper that is more than 3 feet by 2 feet, a size of paper known within the printing business as double elephant folio (Fries 1973). Centered on this massive sheet of paper is an image of a male yellow-billed cuckoo apparently squabbling with a female cuckoo with a beautifully rendered tiger swallowtail butterfly grasped in her bill. The birds are maneuvering through the branches of a pawpaw tree that is laden with ripe fruit, with leaves clearly damaged by leaf miners and black spot fungal disease. The level of detail in the image is astounding, and the lifelike postures of the birds leads one to imagine hearing the wooden, staccato ka-ka-ka-ka-ka-kow-kow-kowlp* of the male as he chases his mate through the tree. Even after the 189 years since it was printed, the hand-painted watercolors are still vibrant and exhibit lifelike subtlety in tone and saturation; the fine engraved lines that capture the feather detail are still razor-sharp and clear. Yellow-billed cuckoo with zebra swallowtail butterfly, Plate 2 from Audubon’s The Birds of America. Digital image created from Clara Peck Collection, Transylvania University. I was introduced to Audubon and his prints by B. J. Gooch, the Special Collections Librarian at Transylvania University, where I am a biology professor. Through her encouragement, I began to take my students into the rare book room to look at our original first edition of Charles Darwin’s On the Origin of Species and to see all of the books written by Alfred Wallace, Darwin’s co-author of the original paper on evolution. Over time, the library tours with my students evolved to include other books and natural history artifacts, ultimately concluding with a dramatic opening of the specially made cabinet that holds the four-volume set of John James Audubon’s magnum opus, the double elephant folio collection of prints titled The Birds of America. As an entomologist, my eye would fix upon the various insects and spiders that Audubon included in his bird portraits. Most striking was that there was often enough detail and accuracy in the engraving that one could easily identify the insect or spider to species, as with the tiger swallowtail in the yellow-billed cuckoo print. After hearing me express my appreciation of the detail in Audubon’s prints, the director of the library encouraged me to identify all of the insects represented in the 435 prints and call the work The Bugs of America. The project ultimately expanded to involve digitally archiving the university’s set of Audubon prints (Fig. 2), because each print is individually hand-painted and each version of an Audubon bird print is unique. I examined each archived print to catalog and identify to the most specific taxonomic level possible all of the insects, spiders, and other terrestrial arthropods represented in the prints. Following on the work of Teale (1947), I then compared each of the final engravings with a facsimile of Audubon’s original paintings, which had been reprinted by the New-York Historical Society (Davidson 1966, Olson 2012). The New-York Historical Society acquired the original paintings when Audubon’s wife, Lucy, sold them in 1863 for $4,000, equivalent to about $1,040,000 today. By comparing the facsimiles of the originals to the final prints, I was able to ascertain which insects were likely drawn by Audubon himself, added later by the engraver Robert Havell, Jr., or painted by other artists who collaborated with Audubon in making the original paintings. Author with student assistant Nikki Fox digitally archiving the original 435 Audubon prints. A special cradle was built to support the binding of the massive books. Photo credit: Susan Brown. As an entomologist, my eye would fix upon the various insects and spiders that Audubon included in his bird portraits. Most people believe that Audubon is the sole artist responsible for an Audubon print, but most of the prints were actually created through a cooperative process with other artists. When I compared the original paintings with the finished prints, I determined that 155 of the 435 prints (36%) are unaltered translations from Audubon’s original painting to the final print. The remainder of the prints either include elements created by other artists Audubon collaborated with, or the final print was altered or finished by the engraver Robert Havell, Jr. During the 12 years in which the prints were created, Audubon employed five different artists, including two of his own sons, to assist in painting the backgrounds. These artists painted the leaves and flowers to represent distinct plant species and to add details such as insects, spiders, and other non-avian animals that would create a sense of place and, at times, drama to the final composition. Because of Audubon’s “idiosyncratic approach to acknowledging assistance” (Lindsay 2018), it is not surprising that most people are unfamiliar with Audubon’s assistants. In the early years of the project (1820–1822), Audubon was assisted by Joseph Mason, an 18-year-old student from Audubon’s drawing school in Cincinnati, Ohio. Joseph Mason traveled with Audubon up and down the Mississippi and Ohio rivers to collect birds and plant specimens and to paint them for Audubon. Mason is thought to have painted 150–200 background watercolors for Audubon, of which Audubon used 56 uncredited (Olson 2012). The other major contributor to Audubon’s prints was Maria Martin, a South Carolinian southern belle and sister-in-law (and later wife) of his good friend Reverend John Bachman. Audubon recognized Maria’s innate talent in painting and tutored her in his method of painting “from nature.” In a short time, Martin progressed from a “skilled fancy worker who painted flowers on handicrafts to an accomplished botanical artist” (Lindsay 2018), and she also painted insects at a level of detail that rivaled that of Audubon. Maria Martin is credited with assisting on 24 different prints, of which five prints (Plates 198, 355, 359, 398, and 416) contain insects she painted. George Lehman was an accomplished landscape painter hired by Audubon to create the scenic backgrounds or detailed botanicals that acted as perches for the birds in 35 of Audubon’s prints. Only two of the prints to which Lehman contributed contain insects: one shows a paper wasp nest that hangs from the white oak branches the Canada jays are climbing on (Plate 107), and the other includes an uncolored beetle-esque form on the underside of a leaf, which is not present in the original watercolor and appears to have been added by the engraver Robert Havell, Jr. Havell was the final engraver for all of the Audubon prints and a talented landscape artist in his own right. As the engraver, he had a great influence on the prints’ ultimate composition and presentation. In fact, when I compared the original paintings Audubon gave to Havell for engraving with the final prints Havell produced, it was evident that Havell had a discernable influence on 168 (39%) of the prints. Havell’s influence ranged from the mundane—altering the composition, adding a small visual element, adding or subtracting background elements—to adding a new bird to the composition. In Mississippi Kite (Plate 117), Audubon instructed Havell to add a female version of the kite to the print by copying it from a print by Alexander Wilson, a competing ornithological artist of the time. In The Birds of America, Audubon envisioned that he was going to accurately portray every bird species in America, which seemed plausible at the time, given that the United States consisted of only about 25 states. To achieve his goal, Audubon traveled and collected bird and plant specimens all along eastern North America, from the Labrador coast in Canada south to Key West in Florida. Audubon found that the most productive areas of collecting were along the Mississippi and Ohio river waterways, where more than 325 bird species are known to migrate that flyway yearly. He travelled frequently on the river from his home in Henderson, Kentucky, to New Orleans, Louisiana. Following the business model of Victorian novels of the time, Audubon serialized his Birds of America as a subscription service: every couple of months, the subscriber would receive five hand-colored engravings—one large engraving, one medium-sized engraving, and three small engravings in a set. Because all of the birds were drawn “the size of life” as Audubon required, the large engravings included birds such as eagles, pelicans, egrets, cranes, swans, and flamingos. Even with the double elephant folio-sized paper, Audubon had to creatively pose the long necks of the flamingo (Plate 431) and anhinga (Plate 316) in oddly serpentine fashions to get them to fit on the page. Medium-sized engravings included ducks, egrets, kestrels, crows, and other crow-sized birds. The small engravings were mostly of smaller passerine birds, but occasionally would include medium-sized birds like a tern or plover. Audubon’s subscription, unlike the Victorian novels of the time, was aimed solely at wealthy individuals, heads of state, universities, and those of royal heritage. It is believed there were 180–200 complete sets sold (Steiner 2003), but the actual final number is challenging to discern, because many individuals joined and quit the subscription during its 12-year run. Originally Audubon planned for the series to comprise 400 prints, with each print representing a single species in a natural life-like pose among species-specific vegetation. As the project progressed, Audubon strove to make his work the definitive bird study. By collaborating with Havell, he increased the project to 435 prints, which allowed Audubon to include the new birds being collected from the western territories. When completed, The Birds of America included 1,065 individual birds drawn to life-size, which represented 489 different bird species. Audubon’s goal was to create a lifelike portrait of each of his bird subjects, a portrait that was more than a scientifically accurate representation of the bird—its form, color, and dimensions—but that also portrayed the bird in its natural environment exhibiting natural behaviors and, to a certain extent, its personality. Audubon also wanted to accurately represent the bird in its natural habitat surrounded by appropriate plants and other non-avian animals. Audubon included other vertebrate animals in his portraits, like small mammals, fish, and other birds that had fallen prey to raptors. When reptiles such as snakes, lizards, and alligators were represented, they were prey for birds or they might be eating birds themselves. Because insects and other arthropods are an important food source for many bird species, it is not surprising that they are often represented in the prints created by Audubon. My survey of the original prints revealed 76 different terrestrial arthropods represented in 67 distinct plates (Supplemental Table, available at https://doi.org/10.1093/ae/tmz066). The level of detail and accuracy of those representations ranges from indistinct ghost blobs with clubbed antennae catching the attention of the female Kentucky warbler (Plate 38) to the cecropia and Io moths being chased by a whip-poor-will (Plate 82), rendered as accurately as one would expect to find in a modern-day field guide. Overall, there are 34 insects represented with enough detail to allow identification to species (Supplemental Table). Not surprisingly, large and colorful Coleoptera (n = 22) and Lepidoptera (n = 17) are most represented within the plates, followed by nearly equal examples of Diptera (n = 7), Hymenoptera (n = 8), and spiders (Araneae, n = 9).
